source.title: Ready2Unlearn: A Learning-Time Approach for Preparing Models with Future Unlearning Readiness
source.authors: Han-Yu Duan; Yi Yang; Ahmed Abbasi; K. Tam

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some characters are garbled, but the relevant recovery results and their descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether fine-tuning on recovery data can restore information after gradient-ascent unlearning, using post-recovery loss as the measure. This is a conceptual test of recovery and resistance, not a reproduction of the cited unlearning methods.
record.gate_note: The paper tests recovery by further fine-tuning on a separate Enron email subset with stylistic consistency to the forget data. Its reported recovery outcomes are post-recovery forget-set loss, not direct accuracy or a count of recovered facts. Figure 7's token-loss illustration and Figure 11's representation visualization do not report recovery behavior as a separate outcome and are not rows. The paper does not test activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompt-only recovery.
record.test_reason: The study proposes a training-time counter-method (Ready2Unlearn) and tests whether gradient-ascent-unlearned LLMs regain forgotten Enron data after fine-tuning on stylistically similar recovery data. Prepared and unprepared models are compared on post-recovery forget loss. This bears on B (loosely related relearning set) and F (a method claimed to resist relearning), though only through cross-entropy loss, not fact recall.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that Ready2Unlearn makes later gradient-ascent unlearning faster, better at retaining utility, and more resistant to inadvertent recovery through similar-style fine-tuning. They frame recovery as unintentional relearning, not an adversarial attack, and attribute resistance to the resilience term pushing the model to forget distinctive, data-specific features.
record.recipe_differences: A training-time meta-learning preparation method followed by gradient-ascent unlearning; it is not one of the cited post-training unlearning methods. Recovery is tested with further fine-tuning on similar-style data.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery-data similarity affects post-recovery loss: the most similar quantile has the highest reported loss for both models. The resilience-term ablation also changes post-recovery loss.
record.peer_reviewed: ACM Transactions on Information Systems (stated in the paper; publication date March 2026)
record.problems: Recovery is assessed through forget-set loss rather than direct recovery accuracy or fact recall, and numeric values for the Figure 6 trajectories are not given. The recovery-set size is not stated. The tabulated language-model recovery results cover GPT-2 and LLaMA-3.2-1B, not all four language models used elsewhere in the study.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible recovery outcomes were left out. Figure 7 and Figure 11 are not separate recovery-attack outcome measurements.

untested.parts: Not tested for LLMs. No targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance, no general-ability benchmark after unlearning, no attack outcome on a standard unlearning method.

Relearning on a subset of the forgotten facts, or on unrelated data. Recovery-set size. Recovery measured as accuracy or fact recall rather than loss. Unlearning methods other than plain gradient ascent.
Not tested. No activation-direction ablation; the t-SNE analysis is not a recovery attack.
Resistance to internal edits, quantization, prompting, and adversarial or forget-subset relearning. Recovery data not seen during training. Models larger than about 1B.

missing.what: Post-unlearning (pre-recovery) forget-loss levels needed to quantify how much is recovered. They exist only as Figure 6 curves, and no row records them.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not one of the original sources. The resistance being measured is inadvertent relearning on data the defense was trained against, which is weaker than robustness to adversarial relearning. Table 3's lambda2=0 arm is a Ready2Unlearn ablation; the text says Table 3 corresponds to Figure 6, so 'without preparation' in Figure 6 may be the ablation rather than Standard Training. That ambiguity is unresolved.

versions.untested_parts: It reports class-wise vision accuracy reaching random guessing and retention, but does not test the full version for LLMs: the LLM results do not report targeted-knowledge accuracy at near chance together with retained general ability and recovery-attack outcomes.

The recovery fine-tuning uses stylistically similar data, but the size of the recovery set is not stated. It does not test unrelated examples, a subset of forgotten facts, or direct accuracy of recovered knowledge.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge is tested.
No low-bit quantization attack is tested.
No recovery through rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or prompt-only information is tested.
Tests resistance to recovery fine-tuning on stylistically similar data only; it does not test resistance to internal edits, quantization, or prompt-only attacks.

relation.reason: Reports forget loss after recovery fine-tuning for prepared and unprepared models.

tranche.reason: Different method (training-time meta-learning preparation plus GA) on the same question of recovery after unlearning by fine-tuning.

source_check.notes: Evidence is forget-set cross-entropy loss only, with no accuracy or knowledge probes. Recovery is inadvertent fine-tuning on same-style Enron data (Drc), which Ready2Unlearn also uses in training. Table 3 is said to correspond to Figure 6 but compares lambda2=3 with lambda2=0, so Figure 6's 'without preparation' curve may be lambda2=0 rather than Standard Training.

statements.correction: Ready2Unlearn: LLaMA-3.2-1B and GPT-2; GA unlearning on Enron emails; recovery by fine-tuning on stylistically similar Enron data (Drc, also used in its training objective); forget-set loss only; prepared models keep higher post-recovery forget loss than unprepared at Epoch 70 (p<1e-12, figure only), but loss still falls during recovery.
statements.problem: Ready2Unlearn is named only in the conditions list. That list's models (7-8B and Gemma-2-2B) leave out both models Ready2Unlearn used, so readers can't see its scale or measure. The 'cuts recovery without removing it' framing fits.

statements.correction: Ready2Unlearn (LLaMA-3.2-1B, GPT-2; Enron; recovery by fine-tuning on same-style data also used in training): converged post-recovery forget loss 5.24 vs 4.69 and 8.04 vs 7.40 with vs without the resilience term (Table 3). Forget loss still falls during recovery (Figure 6). Partial resistance (limits_scope); remove from F support.
statements.problem: Cites R5,R7 as support for F but says nothing about Ready2Unlearn. Its conditions, benchmarks, models and 'why' leave it out (GPT-2, Enron). Ready2Unlearn's resistance is partial and modest, so it belongs under limits, not support.

Fits: the same Drc is an input to Algorithm 1 and the set used for recovery fine-tuning (Section 4.2.1), and forget loss still falls during recovery (Figure 6). Attacks outside that set are not tested for Ready2Unlearn.

statements.correction: Ready2Unlearn (GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B; Enron): each similarity quantile of the recovery set is used separately in Ready2Unlearn, and post-recovery forget loss rises with similarity to the forget set: GPT-2 7.7 (Q1) to 8.5 (Q4), LLaMA-3.2-1B 4.8 to 5.6 (Table 4). Higher loss means more resistance. No unprepared comparator.
statements.problem: Cites R9,R12,R13,R16. Table 4 fits the 'attack data' factor, but the statement does not describe Ready2Unlearn at all. All its numbers belong to other studies.

statements.correction: Ready2Unlearn: with the recovery set in the training-time resilience term (lambda2=3) vs without it (lambda2=0), converged post-recovery forget loss is 5.24 vs 4.69 (LLaMA-3.2-1B) and 8.04 vs 7.40 (GPT-2) (Table 3). Recovery uses that same set. Unseen recovery sets are not tested.
statements.problem: Cites R5,R7 but says nothing about Ready2Unlearn. The citation fits the factor 'attack seen in defence training': lambda2=3 puts the recovery set into the training objective, and lambda2=0 leaves it out.
